title: How to choose between banners, pop-ups, and in-product prompts? UX Guide

UX Guide Riya Jawandhiya 15 min read · Just now -- Listen Share When to use each pattern, what to avoid, and when to stop showing it. In part one, we looked at why promotions compete for attention . The next question is practical: where should each message go? A feature announcement could become a banner , a card , a navigation label , or a dedicated page . Choosing between them means deciding when someone needs the information , whether they chose to see it , and what it asks them to do . Here, I’ve grouped the common patterns by how they enter someone’s work : Interrupting: modals, pop-ups, full-screen takeovers Dedicated: in-product landing pages, upgrade and pricing pages Contextual: cards, banners, feature gates and inline upsells, usage-limit prompts, empty states Ambient: “New” chips, plan labels, usage bars, badges, tooltips Embedded: branding on shared output, milestone moments, free-tier previews Use these as a starting point : a dialog someone opens behaves differently from one that appears uninvited . Last month I logged into 14 SaaS products on the same morning and counted everything on the first screen that was trying to sell me something, teach me something, or pull me away from what I came to do. Yes, a little obsessive. (: Mailchimp had 7 promotional elements on the dashboard. Canva had 5. Shopify Admin had 4. Slack had 3. Notion and Figma had 2 each. Linear had 1. Press enter or click to view image in full size One message, three ways Before the catalog, here’s the example I’d keep in mind while reading it. Say you shipped email sequences . (The copy below is illustrative.) As an unsolicited modal on login. “New: Email sequences. Check it out!” The person has to deal with the announcement before checking their numbers , whether or not email sequences matter to them. The copy doesn’t say what they can do with the feature, either. As a contextual card on the campaign page. “Build a welcome series from your existing template. Email sequences are available now.” It still asks for attention , and possibly action , but it doesn’t require a response before work continues . It sits where someone building campaigns might use it, and it says what they can do. As a page the person opens. A “What’s new” entry with a short demo and a “Try it” button that drops them into the feature. The people who go there chose to, so it can carry as much detail as they want . Same message, three different experiences. The card and the page let the person decide when to engage . The modal decides for them. Tier 1: Interrupting patterns These ask for a response before the work continues . The cost is the switch: reading, judging, responding, and finding your place again. I keep them for messages that can’t wait . Press enter or click to view image in full size Interrupting patterns are also the most resented patterns in product design, and they have the highest engagement per impression, which is exactly why growth teams keep asking for them. Frankly, that number flatters them. It counts dismiss clicks as engagement. Annoyance, logged as interest. Pop-ups and modals Use it when: the message affects what the person is doing right now , or follows something they just did . A dialog they open themselves, like “Compare plans,” appears when requested . An unsolicited one is a different thing , so I count them differently. Common mistake: using one for a routine announcement , or showing it mid-task when someone’s full attention is on their work. Press enter or click to view image in full size When it's not. Routine feature updates ("We added a new chart type!"). Upsells before the user hits a natural upgrade trigger. Seasonal promotions. Anything a banner, card, or tooltip could have carried instead. Cialdini at work: Scarcity (trial ending, limit reached) and Commitment (celebrating a finished onboarding milestone and suggesting the next step). System 1 and System 2. Pop-ups force System 2 to wake up, which is expensive. And here's the trap: System 2 activation doesn't guarantee engagement. It guarantees processing, and "evaluate and dismiss" counts as processing. Over time users build a System 1 shortcut: muscle memory for the X. That's habituation, and it spreads. Products that overuse pop-ups see engagement drop on all their in-product marketing, not just the pop-ups, because the user's brain learns one lesson: this product interrupts me with things that aren't relevant, so dismiss everything fast. Design rules: One pop-up per user per session. Absolute maximum. If you have two things to show, pick the more important one. If someone says "but both are important," that's a prioritization problem, not a design problem. Show it after a task, never during. The user just sent a campaign. Their cognitive budget has a small surplus. That's your moment, not mid-edit with working memory full. Make "Not now" as easy to click as the CTA. Equal visual weight for "Not now&quot
